items.title: Day 1 Overview — Tasks & Competencies
items.body:
Day 1 Overview

Today you'll get comfortable finding your way around Outlook before you start actually using it — the Ribbon, the Folder pane, the Reading pane, the Quick Access Toolbar, and how to get help when you need it. These are the skills you'll lean on every single day this course, in every chapter.

Competencies covered today

  • Identify the elements of Outlook
  • Start the Outlook program
  • Navigate the Outlook screen
  • Get help on Outlook topics

Today's tasks

  1. Watch the Chapter 1 Presentation
  2. The Outlook Window — read, then complete Hands-On OU1-D1
  3. Customizing Outlook — read, then complete Hands-On OU1-D2 & D3
  4. Accessing Help — read, then complete Hands-On OU1-D4 & D5
  5. Chapter 1 Quiz (self-assessment, via eLab)
  6. Chapter 1 Test (via eLab)

items.title: The Outlook Window — Reading
items.body:
Book pages: 2-4 · Chapter 1 · CBO Objectives: Identify the elements of Outlook / Navigate the Outlook screen

Introducing Outlook

Outlook is a personal information manager — it lets you send and receive email, keep an address book of contacts, schedule appointments and meetings, track tasks, and stay organized, all in one program. Outlook has five major elements:

  • Email — send and receive messages, with or without attachments
  • People (also called Contacts) — names, phone numbers, addresses, and contact groups for everyone you communicate with
  • Calendar — appointments and meetings, including ones that recur
  • Tasks — things you need to do, with dates, categories, and reminders
  • Notes — miscellaneous information that doesn't need a due date, like a digital sticky note

Within each element you'll find items — an item is whatever holds information for that element: an email message, a contact, an appointment, a task, or a note.

The Outlook Window

The Outlook screen has three main sections: the Folder pane on the left, the Contents pane in the center, and the To-Do bar on the right (which you can show or hide, and choose what appears on it — Calendar, People, and/or Tasks). The Navigation bar at the bottom of the Folder pane lets you "peek" into Calendar, People, or Tasks and switch between elements.

{{img:pg 3.png|Textbook page 3 — the Outlook Window, labeled}}

The Ribbon

Every Outlook window has a Ribbon with tabs that group related commands — and the Ribbon is contextual, meaning it changes depending on which element or window you're viewing. Opening a new message, for example, shows a completely different Ribbon (Message, Insert, Options...) than the main Outlook window does.

The Folder Pane

The Folder pane shows the contents of whichever element is selected, organized into folders. When Mail is selected, you'll see your mail folders here (Inbox, Sent Items, Drafts, and so on) with a small triangle next to any folder that has subfolders — click it to expand or collapse. One customizable piece of the Folder pane is the Favorites list, which pins folders you want quick access to at the top.

items.title: Hands-On OU1-D1: Explore the Outlook Window & Folder Pane
items.description:
Book pages: 5-6 · Develop Your Skills OU1-D1

Hands-On OU1-D1: Explore the Outlook Window & Folder Pane

  1. Start Outlook (Start button → type OU → choose Outlook from the suggestions).
  2. Watch the Ribbon as you click through the Mail, Calendar, People, and Tasks icons on the Navigation bar at the bottom of the Folder pane — notice the Ribbon's commands change automatically for each one.
  3. Hover your mouse over the Calendar icon (don't click) to see a quick "peek" of your calendar.
  4. Click the Mail icon to return to your Inbox.
  5. Click the View tab, then Layout → To-Do Bar, and turn on both Calendar and Tasks so they display on the right side of the Outlook window.
  6. Click the left-facing caret to minimize the Folder pane, then click it again (now pointing right) to expand it back, and click the push-pin icon to pin it in place.

What to submit

A screenshot of your Outlook window with the To-Do bar showing both Calendar and Tasks on the right side, proving step 5 was completed.

criteria.description: Screenshot shows the To-Do bar displaying both Calendar and Tasks

ratings.description: Full Credit — both Calendar and Tasks are visible on the To-Do bar
Partial Credit — only one of Calendar/Tasks is visible, or the To-Do bar is shown but incomplete
No Credit — no screenshot submitted, or it doesn't show the To-Do bar

items.title: Customizing Outlook — Reading
items.body:
Book pages: 7-9 · Chapter 1 · background knowledge, supports Navigate the Outlook screen

Customizing Outlook

You can customize the look of every Office app you use by setting a theme. The default is Colorful, which matches each program's icon color (blue for Outlook, green for Excel, and so on) — but you can also choose Black, White, or Dark Gray from File → Options → General.

The Reading Pane

The Reading pane displays the actual contents of whatever item is selected in the Contents pane — select a message and its full text shows up in the Reading pane. It can be displayed to the right of the Contents pane, below it, or hidden altogether, and it can be resized by dragging the line between the two panes.

{{img:pg 9.png|Textbook page 9 — the Quick Access Toolbar's More menu}}

The Quick Access Toolbar

The Quick Access Toolbar (QAT) isn't visible by default in Outlook. Right-click anywhere on the Ribbon and choose Show Quick Access Toolbar to turn it on. You can place it either above or below the Ribbon, and the More button at its right edge opens a menu where you can add or remove commonly-used commands, or open More Commands for a bigger list. You can also right-click any Ribbon button directly and choose Add to Quick Access Toolbar.

items.title: Hands-On OU1-D2 & D3: Customize Your Outlook View
items.description:
Book pages: 7-9 · Develop Your Skills OU1-D2 & OU1-D3

Part 1 — OU1-D2: Theme & Reading Pane

  1. Choose File → Options to open Outlook Options.
  2. Under General, set the Office Background to Lunchbox and the Office Theme to Colorful (or another theme of your choice), then click OK.
  3. Choose View → Layout → Reading Pane → Bottom to move the Reading pane below the Contents pane.
  4. Drag the line between the Contents pane and Reading pane to resize it.
  5. Choose View → Layout → Reading Pane → Right to move it back to the right side.

Part 2 — OU1-D3: Quick Access Toolbar

  1. Right-click anywhere on the Ribbon and choose Show Quick Access Toolbar.
  2. Click the More button and choose Show Above the Ribbon.
  3. Click More again and choose Print to add it to the toolbar.
  4. On the Home tab, right-click the New Email button and choose Add to Quick Access Toolbar.
  5. Right-click the New Email button on the Quick Access toolbar and choose Remove from Quick Access Toolbar.

What to submit

Two screenshots: (1) your Outlook Options dialog showing the Background and Theme you chose, before clicking OK; (2) your Ribbon area showing the Quick Access Toolbar displayed above the Ribbon with the Print button visible.

criteria.description: Screenshot 1 shows the Outlook Options dialog with a Background and Theme selected

ratings.description: Full Credit — dialog is visible with both a Background and Theme selection shown
Partial Credit — dialog shown but only one setting is clearly changed/visible

items.title: Accessing Help — Reading
items.body:
Book pages: 10-11 · Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: Get help on Outlook topics

Accessing Help

Where to Get Help

Outlook's built-in Help system is available from the Ribbon's Help tab or by pressing F1. It browses a list of popular help topics, links, training videos, and featured topics, all linked to keywords — searching "folder," for example, surfaces everything related to working with folders.

{{img:pg 10.png|Textbook page 10 — the Help screen}}

Using Instant Search

The Search box above the Ribbon works differently — instead of browsing help topics, it searches live as you type and can suggest the actual command you need, not just an article about it. Typing part of a contact's name, subject line, or an action like "new email" can surface both matching items and the button to perform that action directly.

items.title: Hands-On OU1-D4 & D5: Get Help & Use Instant Search
items.description:
Book pages: 11-12 · Develop Your Skills OU1-D4 & OU1-D5

Part 1 — OU1-D4: The Help Pane

  1. Press F1 to open the Help pane.
  2. Type create new message in the search box and press Enter.
  3. Click the first result to read the topic on creating a new email message.
  4. Click the Home icon in the Help pane to return to the main menu, then click the X to close it.

Part 2 — OU1-D5: Instant Search

  1. Click in the Search box above the Ribbon.
  2. Type new email.
  3. Click New Mail Message under Actions — a new message window opens.
  4. Close the new mail message window.

What to submit

Two screenshots: (1) the Help pane showing your search results for "create new message"; (2) the Search box's suggestions showing "new email" with the New Mail Message action visible.
